citations.review_text:
Um dos meus jogos favoritos, e certamente, um dos melhores jogos da Telltale! Para os que gostam de jogos focados em narrativa onde você escolhe o seu destino, esse é, sem duvidas, muito bom. 

Só não jogue achando que será parecido com Detroit Become Human com dezenas de outcomes. A pegada aqui, por ser um jogo antigo e a Telltale ser uma empresa pequena, boa parte das escolhas levam você para o mesmo caminho e servem apenas para que você possa expressar sua personalidade no Game. Nada disso tira o mérito do jogo ter uma história muito bem escrita e ser bem divertido. Vale a pena!

[h2] 100% Achievement Review #20 [/h2]


● Estimated difficulty: 1/10
● Approximate amount of time to 100%: 13 hours
● Online achievements: none
● Number of missable achievements: 2 in the DLC (Two out of Three, Reunited)
● Difficulty based achievements: none
● Minimum playthroughs: 1
● DLC required: yes, you need the 400 Days DLC
● Glitched achievements: none


[b] Notes [/b]
The first Telltale Walking Dead game is still my favorite story of the bunch, however as much as these games promise choices there really isnt much you can do to influence the story, characters barely remember if you treated them like ♥♥♥♥, the game does not accomodate for when you save a character, they become a background prop after that, not talking at all, just standing there and then die at a later point. All that said I still enjoy the story and the characters, and playing through it after all these years I decided to make Lee into a ♥♥♥♥, which made it that much more enjoyable.

Achievement wise it is a Telltale game meaning you just need to complete the story and you get all the achievements, there is the 400 Days DLC which has 2 missable achievements, one having you win a game of rock, paper, scissors (Two out of Three) and finding one of the dead characters from the main game (Reunited).

nice horror adventure. controls really suck, but good emotionalostory. 
but at the end, story is very linear and choices have not much effect other than the content of later dialogues so I won't buy other other seasons I guess, given the fact that season one is considered the best of all twd episodes.

I've only played through this game once, but it broke my heart and surprised me constantly. Every episode brings fresh ideas that keep you on your toes. Choices really matter here, so pick carefully—and honestly, don't overthink or pause to analyze every option. Just make your calls in the moment for the best experience. The gameplay feels a bit different at first, but it's easy to get used to and isn't overly difficult. Overall, I absolutely loved this game. I cried like a baby at the end, even though I'd already been spoiled for me. Highly recommended.

citations.review_text: The Walking Dead is one of the best story games that I’ve ever played, the comic-book graphics are amazing and even though the game is old it still looks really good today because of the unique art style. The game optimisation is also really good because nearly any PC or console can run it smoothly. In my opinion The Walking Dead is much better than most zombie games because instead of focusing only on action it focuses on characters, emotions and the choices you make throughout the story. I love how every decision feels important and how the game introduces so many interesting characters, enemies and emotional moments that make you care about what happens next. The gameplay is simple but really fun because you get to explore areas, talk to characters, make choices and complete quick-time events during intense scenes. I also love how the game keeps track of your decisions and shows how different characters react to the things you say and do. One of the best parts of the game is the relationship between Lee and Clementine because their story is emotional from start to finish and the voice acting makes every moment feel real. I love the survival theme of the game and how dangerous the world feels the entire time, especially with the walkers always being a threat and the human characters sometimes being even worse. The story is honestly one of the greatest stories I’ve seen in gaming and even though I won’t spoil too much, the ending of Season 1 is one of the saddest and most emotional endings ever made in a video game. The game perfectly shows how much Lee cares about Clementine and how their journey changes both of them throughout the apocalypse. I also love how the later seasons continue Clementine’s story and show her growing up and becoming stronger after everything she went through in the first game. The extras and choice system make the game really replayable because you can go back and change decisions to see different outcomes and character reactions. Overall …

My only regret is that i have discovered this jem of game just month ago.

There are a lot of zombies in the game
THIS GAME IS NOT REALLY ABOUT ZOMBIES, BUT MUCH MORE ABOUT HUMAN BEINGS AND THE CHOICES THE HAVE TO MAKE ON DAILY BASIS NOT TO BECOME INFECTD ZOMBIES OR "HUMAN MONSTERS".

Some of them succeed , but most of them fail and it is very sad and very real at the same time.

There are  bunch of quality fighting zombies , trying to avoid and running away from zombies in the game , but there a lot more social issues, conflicts, judgement and power struggling between tired, hungry and hopeless human beings in the game, and  that what makes the game perfect for me.

Pros:
1. Fascinating Plot - no spoilers here :)
2. Characters authentic look and depth - their clothing, facial expressions, manners, social status...
Excellent  to grab the picture and make first impression that suited very well their behavior during the game.
3. You have no super heroes here  -  just a bunch of regular people with their strengs and flows
4. Variety of characters - by age, gender, race, social and family status...
5. Impact of player desicions on game - your impact is felt very good but main plot still stays valid.
6. For me it was "overwhelming" in a good way. I stopped playing each session not because i got tired of the game, but because I felt need to "process emotions" a bit. Then I got back to it.
7. Can run on almost anything.
I don't have dedicated GPU at all,  only some simple graphic card on motherboard and it is enough to run smoothly.
8. Very good mix of action, investigation, solving, horror and emotions.

Not real deep tutorial but written floating and dissapearing hints - it was good enoough for me and i liked divcing deep immediately but someone would find its lacking.

citations.review_text: I love this game but the save keeps getting corrupted. The Walking Dead: The Telltale Definitive Series might be the better option here over the original.

“A New Day… that still hits hard over a decade later”
I finally wrapped up most of The Walking Dead (Season 1) back in the day — 40/48 achievements (83%), basically everything in the main five episodes plus a good chunk of 400 Days. I played it in chunks across 2012 and 2013, and even now it remains one of the strongest examples of interactive storytelling Telltale ever delivered.
The Good:
•  The writing and characters are phenomenal. Lee, Clementine, Kenny… these people feel real. The choices actually matter (or at least feel like they do), and the emotional gut-punches land every single time.
•  Episode structure is tight. Each one has its own identity and escalating tension. The finale still wrecks me.
•  Atmosphere and music are top-tier for the era. Tense, somber, hopeful in small doses — it nails the tone of the comic/show without just copying it.
The “Meh”:
•  Point-and-click mechanics are dated now. Some puzzles feel a bit arbitrary, and the occasional quick-time event can be clunky.
•  I missed a handful of achievements (probably the more obscure 400 Days ones or specific choice variants), which shows the game has some replay value if you’re hunting 100%, but the story is strong enough that one solid playthrough is very satisfying.
•  If you’re coming in fresh in 2026, know that it’s very much a product of its time visually and mechanically. The Definitive Series version cleans it up nicely though.
This game basically invented (or perfected) the modern narrative adventure for a lot of us. It’s short enough (roughly 10-15 hours for a full run) that you can binge it, yet the decisions and consequences stick with you long after. Clementine’s story across the seasons is legendary, but Season 1 stands on its own as an absolute must-play for anyone who loves story-driven games.
If you like emotional rollercoasters, tough moral choices, and zombies done right (focus on people, not just gore), pick this up. Just make sure you have tissues ready.

citations.review_text:
[b]Choices That Stick & Silence That Hurts – The Walking Dead’s Branching Narrative System[/b]

[i]A choice-driven episodic adventure where dialogue, timing, and moral decisions shape relationships, consequences, and survival in a collapsing zombie apocalypse. [/i]

[b]Core Gameplay & Structure[/b]  
The Walking Dead is built around episodic storytelling split into distinct chapters, each combining exploration, dialogue, and decision-making. You move through small, tightly controlled environments, interact with characters, and advance the story through choices that often feel immediate in impact but long-tail in consequence. The gameplay loop is intentionally simple so narrative weight can take centre stage. 

[b]Choice System & Consequence Design[/b]  
At the heart of the mechanics is the branching dialogue and decision system. You’re frequently forced into time-limited choices that affect relationships, trust, and survival outcomes. The key mechanic isn’t complexity, but permanence — decisions carry emotional and narrative weight, even when the mechanical differences between branches are subtle.

[b]Quick-Time Events & Interaction Layer[/b]  
Action sequences are handled through quick-time events and context prompts rather than free-form combat. These moments inject tension into otherwise narrative-heavy sections, making survival feel reactive and fragile without requiring deep mechanical mastery.

[b]Exploration & Environmental Interaction[/b]  
Exploration is minimal and focused. You examine environments for clues, interact with objects, and trigger conversations that progress scenes forward. The design prioritises pacing and storytelling clarity over open-ended systems or puzzle complexity.

[b]Dialogue & Relationship Systems[/b]

As there are numerous Steam and YouTube reviews of this game, I will not go into too much detail, but TellTale's The Walking Dead [Season One] is their best writing I have experienced and seen. Being the first game in their TWD series of games, it sets the story of a young girl who finds herself caught in the very start of The Walking Dead's apocalypse. While the writing starts to fall apart in the later seasons, this first game is an absolute must experience for anyone who enjoys Zombie/Infected related content, butterfly effect story telling, and/or fans of The Walking Dead franchise. This game beautifully displays consequences for choices made that--although still follow a tightly knit narrative that is mostly the same on every play-through--are felt in specific moments that leave a lasting impact. It may not be as varied as an RPG, but its emotional scenes are no less impactful. 

  As someone who isn't particularly a fan of The Walking Dead, this game had me purchase and play both Seasons Two and even Three. For fans of the franchise, the TellTale games follow closer to the comics than the live-action series, if that is a deal maker or breaker for anyone. For those unfamiliar to TellTales games, it is more of a point and click experience, so do take that into consideration as it is understandably not for everyone.

claims.claim: Reviewers report that the game's advertised choice system creates an illusion of impact, as major narrative branches ultimately converge.

citations.review_text: Arguably, the game that put Telltale Games on the map and reinvigorated the point & click adventure game genre. [i]The Walking Dead[/i] is worthy of the legacy it has today featuring a strong narrative and characters. The only downside is that this is also the game that put the concept of "the illusion of choice" into the broader public eye, and it does not do well in hiding it's narrative railroading.

I want to call this game amazing, but if I were to be a little more objective, it has a great story and endearing characters, but it sucks as a game and player impact on the story is very limited. Nonetheless, I think everyone should experience this classic on their own.

To elaborate, I really have to praise this game. All the characters are extremely memorable and I can remember their faces even 6 years after playing this game for the first time. The story is also solid, I love playing as Lee, a basically adoptive father to Clementine whose entire goal is to protect her, the chapters and general story are also usually solid, except maybe the boat part at the end, but still, if it was a movie or a series, I'd definitely enjoy it.

But it's not without flaws. As a game, it's genuinely such a nothingburger. Quick Time Events and point & click, nothing really extraordinary. Sure, it's an old game, but I prefer when such games have some sort of gameplay to keep the player engaged. Think of, Dispatch with all the dispatching and hacking minigames, or Papers Please/Beholder, which to me is primarily a story about living in a totalitarian country, but also a work simulator, and so on and so forth. And if you can't do that, at least make our decisions matter, like in Detroid: Become Human for example. But nope, whatever decision you do, in a few hours (like the Carlie/Dough choice) or even within seconds (whether to rob the stranded car or nor) whatever you did will be invalidated and the story will continue as usual, without your choice really mattering. Thankfully, Telltale later improved in that regard, but the first The Walking Dead really stands out negatively in that regard.

Also, a minor complaint, Kenny's character is extremely inconsistent. If you didn't almost always stand with him, he's willing to leave Clementine to a psychopatic kidnapper because he's mad at Lee speficically. And also, because uh, spoiler alert? Kenny survives all the way to the end, siding w…

I remember really liking this game back in the day, before I had to sell my PS Vista for groceries. 
In 2026 it's a bit dated and the game play elements are a bit stiff.
But that's not why you play these games. The story is still great though a bit more linear than the "choices" would have you believe. 
The addition of the 400 days DLC is great. Nice to get a glimpse into the lives of other survivors. If you are an achievement hunter, it's a bit annoying that one is based luck. 
All told it was worth my time and I'm looking forward to playing through the rest of the series some time.
